companyCaseStudy.title: How Netflix Cut Metadata Read Latency ~10x with EVCache + Cassandra at 200M+ Users
companyCaseStudy.summary: When Netflix served hundreds of millions of viewers, tiny metadata lookups (profile, recommendations, playback state) were a massive throttle — tens of thousands of reads per second with high tail latency. Using EVCache (a memcached-based distributed cache) in front of Cassandra, Netflix reduced 99th‑percentile read latency from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of milliseconds and cut load on Cassandra by an order of magnitude.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: milliseconds matter at Netflix scale

Netflix streams to 200M+ subscribers worldwide. A 100ms difference in playback-start latency or a slow lookup for personalized recommendations multiplies across millions of requests — and shows up as churn. At peak, thousands of clients were hitting metadata stores every second; occasional 99th-percentile spikes (200–300ms) cascaded into retries, higher CPU, and playback delays.

## Problem: high QPS + high tail latency on datastore

- Workloads: millions of metadata reads per second (profile, recommendations keys, membership flags). 
- Backend: Cassandra clusters storing durable metadata — consistent and highly available, but with higher tail latency under heavy read amplification.
- Symptoms: 99th-percentile read latency of 200–300ms, Cassandra CPU hot spots during peaks, retry storms, and degraded user experience.

### Why simple caching wasn't enough

A single memcached pool or ad-hoc caches caused hotspotting, inconsistent TTLs, and operational complexity. Netflix needed a global, fault-tolerant cache with: consistent hashing, region-aware replication, easy key invalidation patterns, and metrics/telemetry integration.

## Challenge: build a distributed cache that’s global, consistent, and operational at scale

Constraints:
- Multi-region availability (fail over gracefully across AWS regions)
- High hit rates (>85–90%) on small metadata objects
- Low operational overhead (automated failover, telemetry)
- Strong telemetry to avoid cache-miss storms and to tune TTLs

Trade-offs:
- Stronger caching increases staleness risk for certain keys (feature flags, user preferences), so Netflix had to categorize keys by acceptable staleness.
- Replication vs latency: replicate cache data regionally to avoid cross-region hops, accept slightly less global consistency.

## Solution: EVCache — memcached, extended for Netflix scale

Netflix built EVCache: a custom, production-hardened memcached-based layer with features tuned for their use cases:

- Sharded, consistent-hash placement so keys are evenly distributed and rebalanced with minimal churn.
- Multi-region awareness: local reads prefer local cache; asynchronous replication for cross-region resilience.
- Client libraries with built-in fanout/fallback logic — if EVCache misses, code reads Cassandra and writes back the cache (read-through pattern).
- TTL classes & key categorization (hot immutable metadata vs frequently-updated state) to control staleness.
- Extensive metrics: hit/miss/eviction rates and request latencies for automated alerting and tuning.

### Architecture (simplified)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Viewer[Viewer App] --> CDN[CDN/Edge]
  CDN --> API[API Gateway / Edge Services]
  API --> App[Service (recommendation, profile, playback)]
  App --> EVCache[EVCache (memcached clusters)]
  EVCache --> Cassandra[Cassandra (durable backing store)]
  subgraph Observability
    App --> Metrics[Metrics / Tracing]
    EVCache --> Metrics
    Cassandra --> Metrics
  end
```

Flow: App asks EVCache -> hit? return; miss -> read Cassandra -> populate EVCache -> return.

## Implementation highlights

- Read-through pattern: application logic does cache-get → if miss then Cassandra read → cache-set (write-through for warmth).
- Per-key TTL profiles: short TTLs (few seconds) for volatile state, longer TTLs (minutes–hours) for user metadata that tolerates staleness.
- Backpressure and bulkhead: if EVCache is overloaded, services fall back to read-provisioned Cassandra paths with rate limits and prioritized queries.
- Auto-warming: during deploys/evictions, Netflix can pre-warm hot keys into EVCache to avoid initial thundering-herd.
- Monitoring-driven tuning: hit rate, miss storm detectors, and 95/99/99.9th-percentile latencies fed into autoscaling decisions.

## Before vs After (representative numbers)

| Metric | Before (Cassandra-only reads) | After (EVCache + Cassandra) |
|--------|-------------------------------:|----------------------------:|
| Backend read QPS hitting Cassandra | 200k–500k QPS | 20k–50k QPS (≈10x reduction)
| Median read latency | ~20–40 ms | ~5–10 ms
| 99th-percentile latency | 200–300 ms | ~15–40 ms
| Cache hit rate (metadata) | N/A (no warm cache) | 85–95%
| Cassandra CPU utilization during peak | 70–90% with spikes | 10–40% with more headroom

## Results: user-facing and operational wins

- Tail latency drop: 99th-percentile metadata read latency fell from ~200–300ms to ~15–40ms — many user flows (playback start, recommendations) became measurably snappier.
- Reduced backend load: Cassandra read QPS dropped by ~10x for cached workloads, lowering CPU usage and reducing risk of cascading failures.
- Fewer retries and incidents: with lower tails and fewer hot spots, incident volume from metadata-related degradations decreased significantly.
- Operational agility: faster deployments and cache TTL tuning—plus granular metrics—made it easier to reason about trade-offs for staleness vs speed.

## Trade-offs and lessons learned

- Cache invalidation and staleness are real costs. Netflix solved this by classifying keys (stale-ok vs strongly consistent) and only caching the former aggressively.
- Observability is essential. Without high-fidelity metrics, caching can hide problems and create subtle bugs.
- A multi-layer architecture (client + cache + DB) requires robust fallback logic to avoid thundering-herd on misses.

## TL;DR — When to copy Netflix’s approach

- You have many small, high-QPS reads where eventual consistency is acceptable → use a distributed caching tier (EVCache-style).
- You need millisecond-level tail latency guarantees and want to protect durable stores from read storms → put a scalable cache in front.
keyTakeaways: Put a resilient distributed cache in front of durable stores: EVCache cut Cassandra read QPS ~10x and reduced 99th-percentile latencies from ~200–300ms to ~15–40ms.
Classify keys by staleness tolerance and use TTL profiles — aggressive caching without classification causes correctness or UX issues.
Invest in telemetry and fallback logic: monitor hit/miss, detect miss storms, and ensure safe fallbacks to avoid cascading failures.

concept.title: The API Gateway: Your Microservices Traffic Cop (Without Becoming a Bottleneck)
concept.summary: Microservices split responsibilities but put cross-cutting needs (auth, rate-limiting, routing, aggregation) everywhere. An API Gateway centralizes those concerns, simplifies clients, and lets services evolve independently — if you design and operate it right.
concept.explanation:
## Why it matters

Modern apps split functionality across many services. That helps teams move faster, but it creates friction for clients: authentication, rate limits, versioning, request composition, and protocol translation suddenly have to be implemented by every client or sprinkled across services. The API Gateway pattern solves this by putting a single, dedicated "traffic cop" in front of your services to handle cross-cutting concerns.

**Analogy:** Think of an airport. Without a central security checkpoint, every gate would need its own security staff and scanners — passengers and pilots would carry extra burden and security would be inconsistent. An API Gateway is the central checkpoint: one place to validate passports, check carry-ons, and direct passengers to the right gate.

---

## What is the API Gateway pattern?

An API Gateway is a façade that sits between clients and backend services. It exposes a consolidated API surface to clients and handles responsibilities such as:

- Authentication & authorization
- Rate limiting and throttling
- Request routing and load balancing
- Response aggregation (or Backend For Frontend - BFF)
- Protocol translation (e.g., REST ⇄ gRPC)
- Monitoring, logging, and tracing entry points

It intentionally centralizes cross-cutting concerns so backend services can focus on business logic.

---

## How it works (visual)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  Client -->|HTTP/gRPC| Gateway[API Gateway]
  Gateway --> Auth[Auth & Rate Limit]
  Gateway --> Router[Routing & Load Balance]
  Gateway --> BFF[Aggregation / BFF]
  Router --> S1[Service A]
  Router --> S2[Service B]
  S1 --> DB1[(DB A)]
  S2 --> DB2[(DB B)]
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>Gateway: GET /orders
  Gateway->>Auth: Validate token
  Auth-->>Gateway: 200 OK
  Gateway->>OrderService: GET /orders?user=123
  OrderService-->>Gateway: orders payload
  Gateway->>Client: 200 + aggregated payload
```

---

## Before / After (comparison)

| Scenario | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| **Without API Gateway** (Client calls services directly) | Simpler infra, no single extra hop | Clients must know many endpoints, duplicate auth/rate-limiting, tight coupling | Small apps, few services, internal clients only |
| **With API Gateway** | Single entry point for cross-cutting concerns, client simplicity, versioning & protocol translation | Extra network hop, potential bottleneck, operational complexity | Multiple teams, many consumers, mobile/web clients, external APIs |

---

## Alternatives & trade-offs

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| API Gateway | Centralized policy, BFF support, hides complexity | Operationally heavy, single entry point risk | Public APIs, many clients, heterogeneous backends |
| Backend For Frontend (BFF) | Tailored APIs per client (web/mobile), minimal payloads | More services to maintain | When client UX needs differ significantly |
| Client-side Composition | No gateway, clients call services & compose | Lots of duplicate logic, brittle with many services | Internal clients under rapid iteration |

---

## Example: Minimal Node.js Gateway (express + proxy)

A tiny gateway that does simple auth and proxies to an orders service.

```js
const express = require("express");
const { createProxyMiddleware } = require("http-proxy-middleware");
const app = express();

// Simple auth middleware
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (!req.headers["x-user"]) return res.status(401).send("unauthenticated");
  next();
});

// Proxy /api/orders -> orders service
app.use(
  "/api/orders",
  createProxyMiddleware({
    target: "http://orders-service:3000",
    changeOrigin: true,
    pathRewrite: { "^/api/orders": "/" }
  })
);

app.listen(8080, () => console.log("Gateway listening on :8080"));
```

This example demonstrates the basic idea: centralized auth and routing. Production gateways add rate-limiting, circuit breakers, observability, and caching.

---

## When to use an API Gateway

- You have multiple services and many client types (mobile, web, third-party).
- You want to centralize auth, throttling, and monitoring.
- You want to evolve or version backend services without changing clients.
- You need protocol translation (e.g., expose REST while backends speak gRPC).

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

- *Single point of failure/bottleneck*: Run gateways in multiple instances, use load balancing, and autoscaling. Keep gateway stateless when possible.
- *Feature bloat*: Gateways can become monoliths (business logic creeping in). Keep them to cross-cutting concerns; if you need heavy composition for a specific client, consider a dedicated BFF.
- *Complex routing & entangled policies*: Use clear policy definitions (declarative configs), version routes, and automate deployments.
- *Latency amplification*: Add caching at the gateway for common responses and avoid expensive sync operations in the gateway path.
- *Security mistakes*: Gateways often handle secrets and tokens. Use secure storage for keys, short-lived tokens, and audit logs.

---

## Operational checklist

- Automate configuration (IaC) and version your gateway rules.
- Add distributed tracing at the gateway entry so every request can be followed end-to-end.
- Track latency added by the gateway and SLAs for the gateway itself.
- Implement circuit breakers and retries for downstream calls from the gateway.
- Monitor for hot paths and consider moving heavy aggregation into BFFs or async jobs.

---

## Quick before/after example

| Without Gateway | With Gateway |
|-----------------|--------------|
| Clients call /orders-service, /catalog-service, /payments-service directly and implement auth | Clients call /api/orders (gateway handles auth and proxies to orders-service). Easier client code and single token exchange |

---

## Real-world examples

- Kong, Ambassador, Kong Gateway, AWS API Gateway, NGINX, Traefik: popular implementations
- Spotify and Netflix use variants (including BFFs) to tailor endpoints for clients
keyTakeaways: API Gateways centralize cross-cutting concerns so clients and services stay simpler.
They must be designed and operated to avoid becoming a single point of failure or a feature-monolith.
Use a gateway for heterogeneous clients, public APIs, or when you need protocol translation; consider BFFs for client-specific aggregation.
